data.text:
F29 is fixed at records 131 and 132, and verified independently by planting the defect: a
partitioned table in `public` with no `tenant_id` and no row-level security, plus a
partition under it. The suite exits 1 and names both, separately, in all three assertions:
"Tables in the public schema without a tenant_id column: audit_archive, audit_archive_2026",
the same for RLS, and "Policies in the public schema that do not bind the tenant". The
parent is `relkind = 'p'`, so under the old filter it could not have been named at all.

## This one was mine to have caught

F19's round widened the privilege half of the guards to five relation kinds and wrote down,
as a limit it was not closing, that the tenancy half still stopped at `relkind = 'r'`. I
recorded that declaration in note 92 and treated it as acceptable, on the reasoning that
the privilege half closed the exposure. It does not close the criterion. Criterion 2 claims
a test lists every table in the public schema and finds tenancy on 100 per cent of them,
and a partitioned table is a table that the test did not list, so the criterion was
untrue while ticked.

Part 7's classification had already been reading `relkind in ('r', 'p')` at one line since
its own round, four guards away from four that were not, and a comment elsewhere in the
same file acknowledged the gap without closing it. A declared limit is not a closed one,
and a limit that makes an acceptance criterion false is not a limit at all: it is the
criterion being unmet. That is the distinction I got wrong.

## What the fix decided, rather than pasted

The one relkind list became two families with a reason each, which is the part worth
keeping. `TABLE_RELKINDS` is `p` and `r`, the relations whose rows this database's own
policies govern. `NON_TABLE_RELKINDS` is `f`, `m` and `v`, and each is excluded for its own
reason rather than by omission: a foreign table's rows are on another server, so no policy
here decides who sees them; a materialised view can never carry row-level security, which
is why part 6 keeps one out of `public` rather than asking it for a policy; a view is
governed by `security_invoker` instead. Part 4's five-kind privilege self-check stays at
five, because it asks who holds what and not who owes a policy.

Prevention as well as detection, as F19's round did: part 6 now raises when any relation of
kind `p` or `r` in `public` lacks `tenant_id`, enabled RLS or a permissive policy, and the
check was proved non-vacuous against a bad partitioned table rather than assumed.

## The measurement that decides the partition question

Enabling row-level security on a partitioned parent leaves `relrowsecurity` false on the
partition, the policy created on the parent is the parent's alone in `pg_policies`, and
`authenticated` granted select on the partition reads **both** tenants' rows through it
where the same role reading through the parent reads one tenant's. Reading through the
parent is checked against the parent's privileges alone.

So the privilege half is closed by default for a partition and the policy half is not. A
partition is `relkind = 'r'`, so the guards already demand its own `tenant_id`, its own
enabled RLS and its own permissive policy, which is exactly what the guarantee needs. Both
the code and part 6 now say so rather than leaving it to a filter to imply.

## A correction to the briefing this round was given

I told the implementer that part 1's `do` loop reads `relkind = 'r'` and needed widening.
That is not accurate: parts 1, 2 and 3 iterate hard-coded name arrays and resolve each
through `regclass`, which already works for a partitioned table. The relkind filters in the
migrations were three in part 4 and one in part 6. The implementer checked rather than
adopting the claim, which is the behaviour these rounds need.

## Found and not fixed

- `rls.test.ts` (lines 907 and 1099) and `uniqueness.test.ts` (line 219) still read
  `relkind = 'r'`. Those build criterion 3's cross-tenant fixture rather than criterion 2's
  guards, so a later partitioned parent would be skipped by the seeding list and its own
  policy never exercised behaviourally, though its partitions are `'r'` and would be seeded.
  Widening them needs the seeder to know a parent cannot be inserted into before a partition
  exists, which is more than F29.
- No self-check in this set can fire for a partitioned table a later ticket's migration adds,
  because that migration runs after every check here has run. Only an event trigger would
  refuse it at creation, and part 6 declines one for the reason it already gives. The suite
  is what catches it, and part 6 says so.

Criterion 2 stays unticked: it is not the implementer's to tick and not mine, and a review
decides whether the evidence now carries it. F30 and F31 remain open.
